title: Layers and Frequencies
focus: Matrix boundaries, the cache question that is genuinely hard, and the DP that matches patterns.

cards.title: Matrix Traversal
cards.trigger: Walking or transforming a matrix in a geometric order rather than row by row.
cards.recall: Write spiral order from memory with the four boundaries. Then answer: why do the last two directions need an extra guard that the first two do not?
useWhen: Spiral matrix, generate a spiral matrix
Rotate an image by 90 degrees in place
Diagonal traverse of a matrix
Set matrix zeroes using the first row and column as flags
Any layer-wise or boundary-wise matrix walk
template: while top <= bottom and left <= right:
for c in range(left, right + 1): out.append(matrix[top][c])
for r in range(top, bottom + 1): out.append(matrix[r][right])
if top <= bottom:                       # guard: row may be exhausted
for c in range(right, left - 1, -1): out.append(matrix[bottom][c])
if left <= right:                       # guard: column may be exhausted
for r in range(bottom, top - 1, -1): out.append(matrix[r][left])
# Rotate 90 clockwise in place: transpose, then reverse each row
keyInsights: After the first two passes the boundaries may have crossed, so the last two need guards. A single-row matrix is the failing case
Transpose-then-reverse for a clockwise rotation, reverse-then-transpose for anticlockwise. Memorise both directions
Boundary variables beat direction vectors here, because the shrink is what encodes the spiral
cards.trap: 'Set matrix zeroes in O(1) space.' You reuse the first row and column as marker storage, and must handle the first row and column themselves separately. That last part is where people fail.

cards.title: LFU Cache
patterns: Frequency buckets, each an ordered map
cards.trigger: Eviction by usage count, with LRU as the tie-break, all in O(1).
cards.recall: Sketch the three structures from memory before revealing. Then answer the one that makes O(1) possible: how do you find the least-frequently-used item without scanning, and why can `min_freq` only ever increase by one?
useWhen: LFU cache
Any eviction policy combining count and recency
All O(1) data structure, increment and decrement keys
Maximum frequency stack
Any structure needing an O(1) minimum over a changing multiset
template: self.buckets = defaultdict(OrderedDict) # count -> keys, LRU order
if self.min_freq == f: self.min_freq += 1   # only ever +1
if key not in self.vals: return -1
self.min_freq = 1                       # a brand new key resets it
keyInsights: `min_freq` increases by exactly one when its bucket empties, because the item that emptied it moved to freq+1. That is why no scan is needed
Inserting a new key always resets `min_freq` to 1, and forgetting that line is the standard bug
Each bucket is LRU-ordered, so the policy is 'lowest frequency, then oldest'. Two structures, one composed inside the other
cards.trap: 'Why is OrderedDict acceptable here?' Because it is a hash map plus a doubly linked list, which is exactly what you would build. Say that rather than looking like you dodged the work.

cards.title: Level Links Without a Queue
cards.trigger: Connect nodes across a level, and they want constant extra space.
cards.recall: Write the O(1) space version from memory using a dummy head per level. Then answer: what makes O(1) space possible here, when ordinary BFS needs O(width)?
useWhen: Populate next right pointers, perfect or arbitrary tree
Level traversal with constant extra space
Linking siblings in an n-ary tree
Converting a tree into level-wise linked lists
Any BFS where the structure itself can hold the queue
template: # Works for ANY binary tree, O(1) extra space.
dummy = Node(0)          # head of the NEXT level being built
while node:              # walk the CURRENT level via next pointers
node = dummy.next        # descend to the level we just linked
#   node.right.next = node.next.left if node.next else None

problem.name: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node

keyInsights: The already-linked level acts as the queue for the next one, which is why no external queue is needed
The dummy head removes the 'is this the first node of the level' branch entirely
The perfect-tree shortcut is shorter but does not generalise. Write the dummy-head version unless they guarantee perfection
cards.trap: 'Does the recursion count as O(1) space?' No, recursion is O(h) stack. If they said constant space they mean iterative. Say it before they correct you.

cards.title: Pattern Matching DP
patterns: dp[i][j] over text and pattern prefixes
cards.trigger: Match a string against a pattern with wildcards, where a greedy scan is provably wrong.
cards.recall: State what `dp[i][j]` means, then write the star branch. Then answer: for `a*`, what are the two cases, and which one consumes a text character?
useWhen: Regular expression matching with dot and star
Wildcard matching with question mark and star
Interleaving strings
Distinct subsequences
Any two-string matching with optional or repeated elements
template: # empty text can still match patterns like 'a*b*c*'
keyInsights: The star always comes with the character before it, so `j - 2` skips the pair. Treating star alone is the standard mistake
The 'eat one more' branch consumes a TEXT character and stays on the same pattern position, which is what 'or more' means
The base row for an empty text is not decoration. Patterns like 'a*b*' must match the empty string, and the tests check it
cards.trap: 'Now do wildcard matching, star matches any sequence.' Simpler recurrence, and greedy two-pointer with backtracking solves it in O(1) space. Do not reuse this table blindly.

cards.title: Derive an Order
cards.trigger: An ordering is implied by sorted data, and you must reconstruct it.
cards.recall: Sketch the edge extraction from memory. Then name the two failure cases: what makes the input invalid outright, and what makes the derived order non-unique?
useWhen: Alien dictionary, derive an alphabet
Sequence reconstruction from subsequences
Verify an ordering is consistent with constraints
Rank teams by votes, after building a comparison graph
Any 'infer the total order' question
template: indeg = {c: 0 for w in words for c in w}     # every character is a node
for a, b in zip(words, words[1:]):
for ca, cb in zip(a, b):
if len(a) > len(b): return ''        # 'abc' before 'ab' is invalid
q = deque(c for c in indeg if indeg[c] == 0)
keyInsights: Only the first differing character gives information. Characters after it are unconstrained, and adding edges for them is wrong
A longer word before its own prefix is a contradiction with no valid order. That check is easy to forget and always tested
Every character appearing anywhere is a node, even ones with no constraints. Missing them shortens your output and trips the length check
cards.trap: 'Is the order unique?' Only if the queue never holds two characters at once. Same uniqueness test as topological sort, and it is the standard follow-up here.
